items.title: Beyond rules and regulations: How behavioral science is transforming legal judgment, compliance and decision-making
items.summary: In this Leading Questions piece, Raja Sengupta explains how behavioral science can help legal professionals recognize bias, strengthen compliance, improve negotiations and contract oversight, and use AI responsibly while preserving independent judgment. Legal and compliance failures do not always arise from inadequate regulations or poorly drafted agreements. They may also result from cognitive biases, competing priorities, incomplete information, and limitations in individual judgment. For legal professionals, these insights raise an important question: Is understanding the law sufficient, or must effective legal practice also account for how people interpret risks, evaluate evidence, and make decisions? Behavioral science offers a complementary approach to strengthening professional judgment, improving compliance practices, and supporting more informed legal decisions. items.title: Independent directors: A protective mechanism or a false sense of security?
items.summary: During a recent board meeting, a significant related party transaction was scrutinized and subsequently approved. Two years later, this transaction is now subject to investigation by regulatory authorities. Independent directors often perceive Section 149(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 as a safeguard against personal liability. As they are typically not involved in the management or daily operations of the company, this provision limits their liability to matters they were aware of through Board discussions that they either supported or contributed to or in cases where their due diligence was insufficient. However, the necessity for diligence fundamentally alters the interpretation of this provision; it necessitates tangible evidence of actions taken rather than merely serving an honorary capacity upon appointment. items.title: ‘A day off means job loss’: One year on, Surat’s loom workers say labour codes yet to reach them
items.summary: Amit Raut* has been caught in a Catch-22 for nearly two decades. The only work that pays enough to keep his family going is the work that is wearing him down. Raut, about 50, first came to Surat 19 years ago from Ganjam district in Odisha, some 1,600 kilometres away, to work in the city’s power loom factories. Within four years, the pressure and the insecurity amid the clatter of dozens of machines became unbearable. He quit and went home. In Ganjam, he spent nearly 10 years trying to make ends meet as a labourer. Daily wages there could not run a household, and the work was never certain. Three years ago, he came back to Surat, and to the looms. Today he operates power looms in the Katargam area for 14 to 15 hours a day, paid by the metre of fabric he weaves. “I don’t receive any benefits like a labour card, PF (provident fund), or ESI,” he says. Raut’s situation may seem to be an aberration, but it is how a significant portion of Surat’s weaving economy works. The city’s textile trade turns over an estimated Rs 1.5 lakh crore a year, and its looms are run by several lakh migrant workers from Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh. items.title: We investigated why you keep paying for Gurugram’s endless garbage contract
items.summary: Gurugram’s garbage problem was supposed to be solved years ago. Instead, it has become a never-ending cycle of failed contracts and public money going down the drain. Ecogreen was hired in 2017 to collect and process waste in Gurugram and Faridabad. A Chinese company invested Rs 428 crore in the firm, and the government paid Ecogreen another Rs 157 crore. The promised waste-to-energy plant never came and the Bandhwari landfill grew into a much taller garbage mountain, polluting groundwater in nearby villages. Ecogreen was a dormant company owned by the Agarwal family of Ghaziabad until a Chinese firm bought a 99.98% stake in 2017. Within six months, it had won contracts in Lucknow, Gwalior and Gurugram-Faridabad. Company filings show about 80% of the initial Rs 60 crore invested in the Gurugram project went to related parties. Against Rs 428 crore of Chinese investment, only about Rs 60 crore worth of plant and machinery exists on the ground. In 2024, the Chinese firm sold its entire stake for Rs 1 crore and left India.
